---
title: "Comparing two groups"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup}
library(MMSpower)
```

A common question in molecular surveillance is whether the prevalence of a
marker differs between two groups: two regions, or the same region before
and after an intervention. This article plans such a comparison with
`design_difference()` and then analyses the data with `test_difference()`.

Throughout, the scenario is a drug-resistance marker expected at around 10%
in region A (group 1) and 20% in region B (group 2). We want 80% power to
detect that difference at the 5% significance level.

## How many people, with no clustering?

Start with the simplest case: everyone sampled is independent and the
diagnostic test is perfect.

```{r}
des <- design_difference(prevalence1 = 0.10, prevalence2 = 0.20)
des
```

The answer is given per group (`n_per_group`, one value for each group) and
as a total (`n`). With no clustering this is the same calculation as R's
`power.prop.test()`, which gives a fractional answer that
`design_difference()` rounds up:

```{r}
power.prop.test(p1 = 0.10, p2 = 0.20, power = 0.80)$n
```

## One-sided or two-sided?

The default, `alternative = "two.sided"`, looks for a difference in either
direction. If the only result that would change what you do is region A
being *lower* than region B (or, after an intervention, prevalence going
down), a one-sided test is enough, and it needs fewer people:

```{r}
design_difference(0.10, 0.20, alternative = "less")$n_per_group
```

`"less"` means group 1 lower than group 2; `"greater"` means group 1 higher.
Decide the direction before seeing the data. A one-sided test cannot detect
a change in the other direction, however large.

## An imperfect test

If the marker assay misses some true positives (sensitivity below 1) or
produces some false positives (specificity below 1), the measured
prevalences move towards each other. The measured difference is the true
difference multiplied by `sensitivity + specificity - 1`, so a smaller
difference has to be detected and more people are needed:

```{r}
design_difference(0.10, 0.20, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)$n_per_group
```

Sensitivity and specificity are assumed to be the same in both groups. That
is reasonable when the same laboratory and assay are used for both, and
worth checking if they are not.

## Clustered sampling

In practice people are sampled at sites (health facilities, villages or
schools), and people at the same site tend to be more alike than people at
different sites. The intra-cluster correlation (ICC) measures this. The
design effect, `1 + (people per site - 1) * ICC`, says how many times more
people a clustered design needs than an unclustered one.

There are two ways to plan a clustered study. If you know how many people
you can sample at each site, fix `n_per_site` and the function solves for
the number of sites per group:

```{r}
d_per <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
```

Each group needs `r d_per$n_sites[1]` sites of `r d_per$n_per_site[1]`
people, `r d_per$n_per_group[1]` people per group and `r d_per$n` in total.

If the number of sites is fixed instead (for example, the health facilities
already in a surveillance network), fix `n_sites` and the function solves
for the number of people per site:

```{r}
d_sites <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
```

Each of the `r d_sites$n_sites[1]` sites per group now needs
`r d_sites$n_per_site[1]` people, `r d_sites$n_per_group[1]` people per
group and `r d_sites$n` in total.

In both cases `n_eff` is what each group would need without clustering, and
`deff` is the design effect that turns one into the other.

## Groups that differ

The two groups need not share a design. Suppose region B has twice as many
sites in the network, and earlier surveys suggest more clustering there.
Give `n_sites` and `icc` as two values, `c(group 1, group 2)`:

```{r}
diff_des <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites = c(10, 20), icc = c(0.02, 0.05))
diff_des
```

Every element of the result is now a pair of values, one per group. The
people per site is the same in both groups, so region B, with twice the
sites, has twice the people. With the same people per site, its larger
design effect comes from its higher ICC alone, and its `n_eff` is about twice
region A's, in the same ratio as the design.

## When too few sites cannot reach the target

With the number of sites fixed, adding people to each site helps less and
less. Once a site has many people, another person there tells you little
that the others have not, because they share the same local conditions.
However many are sampled, each site is worth at most `1 / ICC` independent
people: with an ICC of 0.05, that is `r 1 / 0.05` people. So 8 sites per
group can never give more than `r 8 / 0.05` independent people per group,
which is not enough for 80% power here. The function says so, and reports
the highest power that design can reach:

```{r, error = TRUE}
design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites = 8, icc = 0.05)
```

Just above the limit, the answer is possible but not sensible:

```{r}
design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites = 10, icc = 0.05)$n_per_site
```

Ten sites can give at most `r 10 / 0.05` independent people per group,
barely above the `r des$n_per_group[1]` needed, so thousands of people per
site are required. If the number of people per site comes out
implausibly large, the fix is more sites, not more people.

## Analysing the data

Once the data are in, `test_difference()` tests whether the prevalences
differ. It takes the number of positives (`x1`, `x2`) and the number tested
(`n1`, `n2`) at each site in each group.

The data below are **simulated**, not real: 20 sites per group with 19
people each (the `n_sites = 20` design above), true prevalences of 10% and
20%, and an ICC of 0.05.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
sim_sites <- function(k, size, prev, icc) {
  # site prevalences vary around prev, with the given ICC (beta-binomial)
  a <- prev * (1 / icc - 1)
  b <- (1 - prev) * (1 / icc - 1)
  rbinom(k, size, rbeta(k, a, b))
}
x1 <- sim_sites(20, 19, 0.10, 0.05)
x2 <- sim_sites(20, 19, 0.20, 0.05)
n1 <- n2 <- rep(19, 20)
x1
x2
```

```{r}
res <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2)
res
```

The estimated difference, group 1 minus group 2, is
`r round(100 * res$difference, 1)` percentage points, with a 95% confidence
interval from `r round(100 * res$ci_lower, 1)` to
`r round(100 * res$ci_upper, 1)`. Since no ICC was given, it was estimated
from each group's own sites (`icc1`, `icc2`) and used to work out the design
effects. An estimated ICC is uncertain, so the test allows for it by using
a t distribution in place of the normal, with `df` degrees of freedom
(about `r round(res$df)` here, worked out from the number of sites in each
group). With few sites per group this makes the test noticeably more
cautious; if a trustworthy value from earlier surveys is available, pass it
with `icc`.

### Score or Wald?

The default, `method = "score"`, is the test that `design_difference()`
sizes for. `method = "wald"` is the simpler textbook test, which works out
the standard error from each group's own prevalence. In large samples the
two agree closely:

```{r}
wald <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, method = "wald")
rbind(score = unlist(res[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]),
      wald  = unlist(wald[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]))
```

In small groups, or with prevalences near 0 or 1, the Wald interval can be
too narrow, so the score method is the safer default. With either method,
the interval leaves out 0 exactly when `reject` is `TRUE`.

### A one-sided test

If the study was planned as one-sided (region A lower), analyse it that
way. The interval is then one-sided too: it runs from -1 up to an upper
bound.

```{r}
one <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, alternative = "less")
unlist(one[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")])
```

### An imperfect test

Correcting for sensitivity and specificity changes the estimated
prevalences, the difference and its interval, but not the p-value:

```{r}
imp <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
rbind(perfect   = unlist(res[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]),
      imperfect = unlist(imp[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]))
```

This is expected. With the same test in both groups, the measured
prevalences differ exactly when the true ones do, so the evidence for a
difference is the same either way. What changes is the size of the true
difference that the measured one implies: the measured difference is
divided by `sensitivity + specificity - 1`, which makes the difference
larger and its interval wider.
